A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same study, with matching authors, tasks, methodology and original experiments. Their text, equations, figures, tables and appendices are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original training experiments measuring sample efficiency, cross-length sharing and length generalization for transformers, LSTMs and Dense-SSMs, including appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original experiments and adds Mamba, Pythia-style and Llama-3-style model evaluations in Figures 6–9.

M1.justification: The binary–geometric search algorithm, sample-efficiency criterion, sharing-factor measure and supervision formats are retained. Added architectures serve as comparison models; they do not modify a proposed method. The revised training budget belongs to the experimental protocol.

E1.justification: Both versions evaluate modular addition, including parity, and S5 permutation composition. The supervision formats, length distributions and length-extrapolation task remain unchanged. New architecture experiments reuse these tasks; chess, code execution and embodied control are discussed without being evaluated.

E2.justification: The cross-length sharing comparisons expand substantially: Figures 6 and 7 add Mamba alongside the original transformer, LSTM and Dense-SSM, while Appendix B.4 compares GPT-2-style transformers with Pythia- and Llama-3-style variants on both tasks. Tables 1–4 retain their original comparator sets.

E3.justification: Section 2 and Appendix A.1 replace a fixed 250,000-step budget with at most 250,000 steps and early stopping upon meeting the validation-loss criterion. A.1 corrects the sample-space count to start at length 2. B.4 adds matched architectural controls. These reported changes do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix B.4 directly tests whether the central sharing findings are specific to GPT-2, using matched Pythia- and Llama-3-style architectures across both tasks and all three supervision formats. This substantially extends architectural robustness analysis. Existing length-generalization and smaller-model analyses remain.

E5.justification: Both versions use the same five seeds, three learning rates and success criterion based on any successful configuration. Neither introduces confidence intervals or significance tests. The increase from over 190,000 to over 200,000 total training runs does not indicate increased repetitions per condition.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 retain their numerical results, but Figures 6–9 substantially expand sharing results. Mamba's modular-addition sharing factors are 3.62, 0.30 and 2.56 for outcome supervision, CoT and ACoT. New Pythia/Llama-3 results include outcome-supervision factors of 2.60/5.79 and CoT factors of 0.22/0.36. These are additional model results, not improvements to retained models.

T1.justification: Section 1 revises the formal induction-bias condition: the right-hand conditional distribution depends on h_t alone in v2, rather than on both x_t and h_t in v1. Appendix A.1 also corrects the sequence-count summation's lower limit from 1 to 2. No new theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The abstract, introductory contribution statements and main conclusion retain the claims about transformer data inefficiency, weak cross-length sharing and recurrent induction bias. Added architecture experiments support or test these existing claims; they do not redefine the central contribution.

C2.justification: v2 extends the destructive-interference interpretation to Mamba and discusses its intermediate sharing behavior. The conclusion replaces confidence about slight model variations with more explicit synthetic-task limitations and unresolved transfer to realistic domains. Section 3 also clarifies that fitted curves are visual guides.

D1.justification: Appendix A.3 adds Mamba implementation details, including expansion factor 2, state size 64 and convolution kernel size 4. B.4 specifies matched transformer dimensions, attention heads, MLP sizes and rotary positional embeddings. The stopping description and aggregate training-run count are also updated.

R1.justification: Related work adds substantive connections to Chang and Bisk's inductive counting study and Marchetti et al.'s sequential group-composition work. References for Mamba, Pythia and Llama 3 support the added comparisons. The overall positioning around in-distribution efficiency remains unchanged.

P1.justification: v2 expands related work and the group-theoretic task explanation, rewrites the limitations paragraph, adds Appendix B.4 and makes local terminology and grammar edits. The main section order and overall narrative structure remain intact.

P2.justification: The comparative visualization expands substantially: Figures 6 and 7 grow from three to four model columns, and new nine-panel Figures 8 and 9 compare transformer variants. Figure 2 extends its vertical scale from 10,000 to 50,000, revealing previously clipped observations. Existing tables are retained, while several figures move and observation boxes are restyled.

improvement.justification: The added architecture comparisons directly address v1's reliance on one transformer design, while clearer implementation information and synthetic-task limitations improve transparency. The gain is limited by incomplete reconciliation of the new evidence with retained claims: Figure 8 reports meaningful Llama-3 sharing, including 5.79 under outcome supervision, despite the broad claim of negligible transformer sharing. The revision strengthens the evidence more than it refines the conclusions.
